design_clause: §6 P2 — separator expressibility. For ten hand-sealed ambiguous prompts: does any single admitted command distinguish the rival readings under exact evaluation? If no separator exists for most, the clarifying-question arm has nothing to ask and the conditional-answer arm wins by measurement. Committed either way.
authored_by: maintainer, by hand, before any probe was written or run
what_a_prompt_is: prose a person might plausibly type at the harness prompt, whose reading is ambiguous between two or more ADMITTED COMMANDS of the registered line grammar. The prompt itself is not required to route anywhere; the readings are.
what_a_reading_is: one line of the registered grammar (serve_chat.LINE_GRAMMAR row named per reading) that the prompt could plausibly have meant. A reading is not a paraphrase of the prompt — it is a command the system already admits.
sealing_rule: the prompts and their candidate-reading sets are frozen in THIS file before the probe exists. The probe reads this file and may not add, drop, or reword a reading; scripts/probe_separator_expressibility.py digests these bytes and carries the digest into its own artifact so a reader can check that the question was written before the answer.
authoring_constraint: no reading was executed while this file was being written. Rows whose reading depends on an optional subsystem are sealed anyway and the probe records whether that subsystem registered on the measuring boot, rather than the seal quietly avoiding them.
non_claims: no claim that these ten are representative of what any person types — they are maintainer-authored, and STRANGER's park (docs/ROADMAP-v0.20.md:394) is cited rather than re-encountered
no completeness claim over readings: a prompt's candidate set is what one author could see, and DESIGN-session-ledger §11 forbids the completeness claim outright
no claim that a separated pair is a pair a person would want distinguished

amendments.what_changed: the `grammar_row` integer on 19 of the 25 readings, from the index the row held when this seal was written to the index it holds now.
amendments.what_did_not_change: the sealed QUESTION. Not one prompt, `why_ambiguous`, reading `command`, reading `route` or reading `gloss` is touched. The route names are what identify a reading's grammar row; the integers were derived pointers to them.
amendments.why: v0.21's session ledger added a `retract <assumption-id>` row to serve_chat.LINE_GRAMMAR — required by DESIGN-session-ledger §3's Assumption status alphabet, which registers `retracted` and had no word for it. Inserting it shifted every row after `suppose` by one, so every integer at or above 4 in this file became wrong.
amendments.why_corrected_in_place_rather_than_annot: the deciding question this repository asks about a repair is what it costs the reader's ability to check. This seal is hand-authored, so its bytes are not a reproduction proof that a note would destroy; and a wrong integer in a canonical artifact is a false sentence that a note a reader may never open cannot repair. The precedent is the v0.20 conformance review's in-place correction, not the voice review's untouched byte-reproduced artifact.
amendments.consequence: scripts/probe_separator_expressibility.py now resolves a reading's row by ROUTE NAME rather than by index, so the same shift cannot silently mis-read this file again, and the probe artifact was recomputed against the current grammar.

amendments.what_changed: two `harness.py:NNNN` line citations inside `why_ambiguous` prose, refreshed to the lines they were always about.
amendments.what_did_not_change: nothing else. No prompt, no reading `command`, no `route`, no `gloss`, no `grammar_row`.
amendments.why: v0.21's own work added lines to scripts/harness.py, so `harness.py:2109-2113` (the routing chain putting the corpus before the dictionary) and `harness.py:2083-2091` (the suppose line that binds and computes being routed to evaluate first) both pointed past their targets. A citation that points at the wrong lines is a false sentence, and this repository's rule is that a false sentence in a canonical artifact cannot be repaired by a note a reader may never open.

citations_corrected.about: route_line reaching the resolver before the gloss route
a suppose line that binds and computes routed to evaluate first

amendments.note_on_line_citations_generally: they rot whenever the cited file grows, which is why this repository's reviews keep finding them. Nothing here depends on them: the seal's meaning is carried by its prompts, commands and route names, and the citations are courtesy pointers.

amendments.what_changed: two readings gain a `predicted_fallthrough_route` field, making machine-readable a prediction the seal's own prose already carried.
amendments.what_did_not_change: no prompt, no reading `command`, no `route`, no `gloss`, no `why_ambiguous`, no `grammar_row`. Nothing about the sealed QUESTION.
amendments.why: the probe counted a reading as 'routed where the seal said' only when the served route equalled the reading's `route` field, and reported 19 of 25. Independent review found that wrong by two: for p05.evaluate and p06.spend the seal had ALREADY PREDICTED IN WRITING that they would fall through, and p06's prediction is the very ambiguity the prompt was sealed to exhibit. Counting a reading the seal predicted correctly as a reading that surprised it makes the metric measure the seal's field layout rather than its foresight.
amendments.consequence: readings_that_routed_where_the_seal_said reads 21 of 25 rather than 19, and the probe now publishes readings_that_surprised_the_seal beside it so both are visible. The four genuine surprises remain: p02.gloss (the offline boot forces its subsystem OFF), p07.belief and p07.resolver (both fall to the dispatcher), p08.resolver.
